results.title: Reproducibility and Artifact Evaluation
results.content: # Reproducibility and Artifact Evaluation. To address this, PADS has joined the group of ACM conferences that have established an optional reviewing process to evaluate artifacts and reproduce computational results. The goal of the Artifact Evaluation process are manifold:. * to reward authors who take the trouble to create useful documentation and artifacts beyond the paper. The Reproducibility Committee (RC) will read the paper and judge how well the artifacts match these criteria. In accordance with ACM Artifact Review and Badging, some of the following ACM badges may be applied, and stamped on the final paper published in the proceedings. Authors have created artifacts relevant to this paper have been placed on a publicly accessible archival repository. In particular, the main results of the paper have been obtained in a subsequent study by a person or team other than the authors, using, in part, artifacts provided by the author. To maintain a wall of separation between paper review and the artifacts, the evaluation process will only start after the corresponding paper is accepter. By no means, the Artifact Evaluation initiative will have an impact on the acceptance of papers, meaning that authors who opt in will not have higher changes of having their work accepted, nor failing at reproducing the results will have an impact on the acceptance of the paper. The artifacts will be evaluated in relation to the expectations set by the paper. * *Artifact assessment*: reviewers evaluate the artifacts, checking if they live up to the expectations created by the paper. At the end of the process, reviewers will prepare a report (to be published in the proceedings) including a discussion of the artifact evaluation process. More than one badge could be applied to each paper, depending on what expectations on the artifacts are met. To avoid excluding some papers, the RC will try to accept any artifact that authors wish to submit. Please note that the SIGSIM PADS Artifact Evaluation initiative is an open reviewing process in which both reviewers and authors are known to each other. * A README file, describing the artifacts associated with the paper (e.g., data, simulation models, …).

results.title: The Giants Are Hungry — And That’s Exactly Where You Should Be Hunting | by ABV | Medium
results.content: There’s a tired chest-thump you’ll hear in investor bars and Slack channels: ***“AI founders are idiots — corporations will eat their business models.”*** It sounds dramatic and, to be frank, a little smug. **Yes**: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and others now own much of the plumbing — models, cloud contracts, and distribution channels. I’ll show why the market will polarize (models/clouds vs overlays), why structured intensity (accelerators, hard metrics, repeatable product loops) improves survival, and why reproducibility engineering is now a first-class product feature. ## Why the Giants Matter — and Why That’s Not the End of the World. 2. **Model & infrastructure control.** Owning or licensing the base LLMs — plus the cloud contracts and compute scale required — gives incumbents cost and integration advantages. ***Opportunity remains because the upper layer — the overlays — will be productive real estate: vertical SaaS, narrow agents, country-/language-specific solutions, and tool-integrations. * **The Axis (monopolies & platforms):** Large cloud vendors and model providers — Microsoft (Copilot & M365), Google (Gemini in Search/Android), OpenAI — owning base models and tight distribution hooks. That’s why reproducibility engineering — seeds, deterministic ops, hashed datasets, CI for ML — becomes a seller’s feature, not an academic footnote. 3. **Fast feedback loops:** choose a market where you can trial and measure impact quickly (pilot with 1–3 customers, measure outcomes in 1–4 weeks). ## The Accelerator Playbook — Apply, Iterate, Repeat. * **Deterministic outputs:** reproducibility again — buyers value predictability. Building with clean engineering, predictable outputs, and customer-impact metrics makes both paths — scale or exit — possible.***. * **Month 3–6:** Apply to accelerators, iterate on feedback, show improved metrics. * **Month 12–24:** Close a seed or pre-seed with pilots backing it — or grow MRR and become attractive for early strategic buyers. Focus on being the surgical tool they can’t spare: a vertical product that moves a measurable metric and integrates cleanly into the workflows giants already own. Be buyable — but build something that customers will cry for first. Apply to accelerators, keep a short metric horizon (1–4 weeks per experiment), and don’t confuse noise with signal.***.

results.title: Seqera Launches Seqera Containers to Enable Bioinformatics Reproducibility and Innovation
results.content: # **Seqera Launches Seqera Containers to Enable Bioinformatics Reproducibility and Innovation**. *Free, publicly available container solution supported by and built on AWS allows users to create custom on-demand container images to support scientific collaboration and discoveries*. NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Seqera, the leading software provider for complex data analysis in the life sciences space, today announced the launch of Seqera Containers, a no-cost, streamlined bioinformatics container solution, during their second annual Nextflow SUMMIT in Boston. This publicly available project creates a simplified experience, allowing developers and researchers to effortlessly assemble containers tailored to their needs without having to build and upload custom container images. Powered by Amazon Web Services (AWS), this solution assembles on-demand containers via Wave, Seqera’s open-source, next-generation container provisioning service. “Seqera Containers enable reproducibility, scalability, and collaboration in bioinformatics research, easing the burden of software management so researchers can focus on core scientific endeavors. With the inclusion of this solution into our platform, we’re on track to create a centralized hub for scientists’ every analytical need, supporting them with access to a community of their peers to enhance research and accelerate the pace of discoveries.”. Containers assembled on-demand through Seqera are publicly accessible to the entire user community, empowering scientists with seamless access to bioinformatics resources. Images requested through the Seqera Containers web interface can be accessed instantly with consistent reuse across organizations by anyone in the community. It also ensures the reproducibility that is so crucial to scientific research while minimizing the burden of creating custom containers. To learn more about Seqera Containers and its capabilities, visit: Additional information about Seqera can be found at. Seqera makes complex data analysis accessible at any scale by providing the tools to drive innovation in genomics, global health, and beyond. Today, Seqera consolidates fragmented data and diverse computing resources into a unified platform. results.title: Reproducibility and Artifact Consistency of the SIGIR 2022 Recommender Systems Papers Based on Message Passing
results.content: Computational and data-intensive sciences (Freire et al., 2016; National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2019) are no exception, and this is also true for *Information Retrieval* (IR) and *Recommender Systems* (RS) (Breuer et al., 2020a; Ferrari Dacrema et al., 2019; Ferro, 2017; Lin, 2022), especially considering how both fields are heavily reliant on machine learning approaches today (Lucic et al., 2022) and how reproducibility is a concern for machine learning itself (Gibney, 2020; Pineau et al., 2021). Given the general interest in graph-based techniques for RS, the surge of papers on this topic at SIGIR, and the previous experiences and concerns of the IR and RS communities regarding reproducibility and weak baselines, the question of whether the reproducibility of the results and reliability of the experimental methodology has improved naturally arises and papers addressing these questions are starting to appear, e.g., Anelli et al.
